source_text: Εἰ γὰρ αὐτός ἐστιν ἡ ζωὴ, πῶς ἡ ζωὴ ζωὴν λαμβάνει; Καὶ εἰ αὐτὸς ἐπαγγέλλεται λέγων· Τὰ πρόβατά μου τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούει, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτὰ, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσί μοι, κἀγὼ ζωὴν αἰώνιον δίδωμι αὐτοῖς, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀπόλλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα· καὶ εἰ αὐτός ἐστιν ἡ σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ εἰ αὐτὸς ἐποίησε πᾶσαν ἡλικίαν, πῶς λέγεται· Προέκοπτε δὲ Ἰησοῦς σοφίᾳ καὶ ἡλικίᾳ; Καὶ εἰ ὁ Πατὴρ διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου Λόγου καὶ Υἱοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐποίησε, δῆλον, ὅτι καὶ τὴν ἔγερσιν τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ δι' αὐτοῦ ἐποίησε. Δι' αὐτοῦ οὖν αὐτὸν ἤγειρε, καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ αὐτῷ ζωὴν δίδωσιν. Ἐγείρεται μὲν κατὰ σάρκα ὡς ἄνθρωπος, καὶ λαμβάνει ζωὴν ὡς ἄνθρωπος, ἐν σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος. Καὶ αὐτὸς δέ ἐστιν ὁ ἐγείρων τὸν ἴδιον ναὸν, ὡς Θεὸς, καὶ διδοὺς ζωὴν τῇ ἰδίᾳ σαρκί. Ὅταν οὖν πάλιν λέγῃ, Ὃν ὁ Πατὴρ ἡγίασε, καὶ ἀπέστειλεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον, ἀλλαχοῦ φησιν· Ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐγὼ ἁγιάζω ἐμαυτὸν, ἵνα ὦσι καὶ αὐτοὶ ἡγιασμένοι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ· καὶ ὅταν λέγῃ· Θεέ μου, Θεέ μου, ἵνα τί με ἐγκατέλιπες; ἐκ προσώπου ἡμετέρου λέγει· διότι μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν, καὶ ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν, γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, θανάτου δὲ σταυροῦ, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. Καὶ καθὼς λέγει Ἡσαΐας· Αὐτὸς τὰς μαλακίας ἡμῶν αἴρει, καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται· ὥστε οὐχ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ ὀδυνᾶται, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν· καὶ οὐκ αὐτὸς ἐγκατελείφθη ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλ' ἡμεῖς, καὶ δι' ἡμᾶς τοὺς ἐγκαταλειφθέντας παρεγένετο εἰς τὸν κόσμον. Καὶ ὅτε λέγει· Διὸ καὶ ὁ Θεὸς αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσε, καὶ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ ὄνομα, τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα, περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ λέγει, ὅ ἐστι τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ. 989 Οὐ γὰρ ὁ Ὕψιστος ὑψοῦται, ἀλλ' ἡ σὰρξ τοῦ Ὑψίστου ὑψοῦται· καὶ τῇ σαρκὶ τοῦ Ὑψίστου ἐχαρίσατο ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα. Καὶ οὐχ ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ χάριν ἔλαβε τὸ καλεῖσθαι Θεὸς, ἀλλ' ἡ σὰρξ αὐτοῦ σὺν αὐτῷ ἐθεολογήθη. Οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν, ὅτι ὁ Λόγος Θεὸς γέγονεν, ἀλλὰ, Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος· Ἀεὶ ἦν, φησὶν, ὁ Θεὸς Λόγος, καὶ οὗτος αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς γέγονε σὰρξ, ἵνα ἡ σὰρξ αὐτοῦ γένηται Θεὸς Λόγος· καθὼς καὶ ὁ Θωμᾶς, ψηλαφήσας τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ, ἀνεβόησεν· Ὁ Κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ Θεός μου, τὸ συναμφότερον θεολογῶν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ Ἰωάννης ἔγραψεν· Ὃ ἦν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ὃ ἀκηκόαμεν, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἡμῶν, ὃ ἐθεασάμεθα, καὶ αἱ χεῖρες ἡμῶν ἐψηλάφησαν περὶ τοῦ Λόγου τῆς ζωῆς. Φανερὸν οὖν ἐστιν, ὅτι ἐν σαρκὶ ὁ Υἱὸς καὶ Λόγος τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐψηλαφήθη, καὶ τὸ συναμφότερον, Λόγον ζωῆς, ἡ θεία Γραφὴ παραδέδωκε ψηλαφηθέντα. Καὶ ὅτε λέγει· Οὔπω ἦν Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς οὐδέπω ἐδοξάσθη, τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ λέγει μήπω δοξασθεῖσαν. Οὐ γὰρ ὁ Κύριος τῆς δόξης δοξάζεται, ἀλλ' ἡ σὰρξ τοῦ Κυρίου τῆς δόξης· αὕτη λαμβάνει δόξαν συναναβαίνουσα αὐτῷ εἰς οὐρανόν. Ὅθεν καὶ Πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας οὔπω ἦν ἐν ἀνθρώποις, διότι ἡ ληφθεῖσα ἀπαρχὴ ἐξ ἡμῶν οὔπω ἦν ἀνελθοῦσα εἰς οὐρανόν.
thought_title: The Son's humble sayings and experiences belong to his flesh, not his divinity
orientation: Marcellus is explaining that when Scripture says the Son was raised, given life, sanctified, forsaken, or exalted, these things are said of his assumed flesh, not of the eternal Word.
pass_a_gloss: For if he himself is the life, how [does] the life receive life? And if he himself promises saying: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give eternal life to them, and they will never perish into the age; and if he himself is the wisdom of God, and if he himself made all age, how [is it] said: And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age? And if the Father through [his] own Word and Son made all things, [it is] clear, that also the raising of his flesh through him he made. Through him therefore he raised him, and through him to him he gives life. He is raised according to flesh as man, and receives life as man, in form found as man. And he himself is the [one] raising [his] own temple, as God, and giving life to [his] own flesh. When therefore again he says, Whom the Father sanctified, and sent into the world, elsewhere he says: On behalf of them I sanctify myself, that they may be also themselves sanctified in truth; and when he says: My God, my God, why did you forsake me? from [the] person of us he says; because [the] form of a slave taking, and in likeness of men becoming, and in form found as man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient until death, and death of a cross, and the [things] following. And just as Isaiah says: He our weaknesses bears, and about us suffers pain; so that not on behalf of himself he suffers pain, but on behalf of us; and not he himself was forsaken by God, but we, and on account of us the [ones] forsaken he came into the world. And when he says: Therefore also God him highly exalted, and granted to him a name, the [one] above every name, about the temple he says, which is the body of him. For not the Highest is exalted, but the flesh of the Highest is exalted; and to the flesh of the Highest he granted a name the [one] above every name. And not the Word of God according to grace received the [being] called God, but his flesh with him was called God. For he did not say, that the Word became God, but, God was the Word; Always he was, he says, the God Word, and this same God became flesh, that his flesh may become God Word; just as also Thomas, touching the flesh of him, cried out: My Lord, and my God, the both together calling God; likewise also John wrote: What was from [the] beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we beheld, and our hands touched about the Word of life. [It is] clear therefore, that in flesh the Son and Word of the Father was touched, and the both together, Word of life, the divine Scripture has handed down [as] touched. And when he says: Not yet was [the] Holy Spirit, because Jesus not yet was glorified, the flesh of him he says not yet glorified. For not the Lord of glory is glorified, but the flesh of the Lord of glory; this receives glory going up with him into heaven. Whence also [the] Spirit of adoption not yet was in men, because the taken firstfruit from us not yet was gone up into heaven.

lemmas.gloss: was declared God, was spoken of as God

choices.why: The context is Jesus advancing in wisdom and age, paired with wisdom as a human growth; 'age' keeps the temporal sense of the Greek rather than physical stature.
The glossary requires 'form of a servant' for this key term, preserving the Pauline phrase exactly.
The verb means to speak of as God; 'declared God' captures the passive sense that the flesh was spoken of as God together with the Word, not that it became divine by nature.
This rare term means both things taken together; 'the whole together' preserves the sense that Thomas and John confess the flesh and the Word as one whole, not two separate things.
The glossary requires 'firstfruits' for this term, used of Christ's flesh as the first portion of humanity taken up into heaven.
The glossary requires 'adoption' for this term, the gift by which human beings become children of God.

pass_b_english: For if he himself is the life, how does the life receive life? And if he himself promises, saying, "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish into the age" (John 10:27-28), and if he himself is the wisdom of God, and if he himself made every stage of growth, how is it said, "Jesus advanced in wisdom and age" (Luke 2:52)? And if the Father made all things through his own Word and Son, it is clear that he also accomplished the raising of his flesh through him. Through him, then, he raised him, and through him he gives him life. He is raised according to the flesh as a human being, and he receives life as a human being, having been found in appearance as a human being. And he himself is the one who raises his own temple as God, and who gives life to his own flesh.

When, then, he again says, "The one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world" (John 10:36), he says elsewhere, "For their sake I sanctify myself, so that they also may be sanctified in truth" (John 17:19). And when he says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46), he speaks from our own person, because having taken the form of a servant and having become in the likeness of human beings, and having been found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:7-8), and so on. And as Isaiah says, "He bears our weaknesses and suffers pain for us" (Isaiah 53:4), so that he does not suffer pain for himself but for us. And he was not forsaken by God, but we were; and for us who had been forsaken he came into the world.

And when he says, "Therefore God highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name" (Philippians 2:9), he speaks about the temple, which is his body. For the Most High is not exalted, but the flesh of the Most High is exalted; and to the flesh of the Most High he granted the name that is above every name. And the Word of God did not receive by grace to be called God, but his flesh together with him was declared God. For he did not say that the Word became God, but "the Word was God" (John 1:1). He was always, it says, God the Word, and this same God became flesh, so that his flesh might become God the Word (John 1:14). Just as Thomas, having touched his flesh, cried out, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), declaring the whole together as God. In the same way John also wrote: "What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at, and our hands have touched concerning the Word of life" (1 John 1:1). It is clear, then, that the Son and Word of the Father was touched in the flesh, and the divine Scripture has handed down that the whole together—the Word of life—was touched.

And when he says, "The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified" (John 7:39), he means that his flesh was not yet glorified. For the Lord of glory is not glorified, but the flesh of the Lord of glory is; this flesh receives glory as it ascends with him into heaven. Therefore the Spirit of adoption was not yet among human beings, because the firstfruits taken from us had not yet gone up into heaven.

problems.quote: if he himself made every age
problems.why: ἡλικία here means bodily stature/growth, not 'age'; parallel to Luke 2:52 'advanced in wisdom and ἡλικίᾳ.'
problems.fix: if he himself made every stage of growth
problems.ruling: ἡλικίαν in Luke 2:52 parallel refers to bodily stature/growth, not temporal 'age'; 'every age' misrepresents the argument about Jesus creating growth yet growing.

edits.old: if he himself made every age
edits.new: if he himself made every stage of growth

fixed: Changed 'every age' to 'every stage of growth' because ἡλικία here refers to bodily stature/growth, parallel to Luke 2:52.

problems.quote: having been found in appearance as a human being
problems.why: σχῆμα means 'form' or 'outward form,' not 'appearance' in the sense of visual look. The glossary specifies 'form of a servant' as μορφὴ δούλου. Here σχήματι is the dative of σχῆμα, meaning 'in form'—the outward form/shape. 'Appearance' is weaker and could mislead.
problems.fix: having been found in form as a human being

problems.source_quote: καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀπόλλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
problems.why: Source adds 'into the age/forever'; English omits this phrase.
problems.fix: and they will never perish into the age
problems.ruling: Source has 'εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα' (into the age/forever); English omits this phrase entirely, losing meaning.

problems.quote: the right to be called God
problems.why: τὸ καλεῖσθαι Θεὸς means 'to be called God' or 'the being called God,' not 'the right to be called God.' The English adds 'right' which is not in the Greek and changes the meaning—it's about actually being called God, not having permission.
problems.ruling: τὸ καλεῖσθαι Θεὸς is 'to be called God,' not 'the right to be called God'; adding 'right' changes meaning.

last_rejected.quote: declaring the whole together as God
last_rejected.why: 'Declaring the whole together as God' is awkward and unclear. The Greek τὸ συναμφότερον means 'the combination of both' or 'both together' — i.e., both natures, divinity and humanity. 'The whole together' is not standard English and obscures the theological point that Thomas confesses both natures as God. 'Declaring both together to be God' or 'confessing the combination as God' would be clearer.
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ συναμφότερον = 'the whole together'; 'declaring...as God' renders θεολογῶν adequately. Stylistic preference only.

last_rejected.quote: he speaks from our own person
last_rejected.why: 'From our own person' is ambiguous. The Greek ἐκ προσώπου ἡμετέρου means 'in our person' or 'on our behalf' or 'representing us.' 'From our person' suggests derivation rather than representation. 'In our person' or 'on our behalf' would better capture the vicarious nature of Christ's words.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκ προσώπου ἡμετέρου = 'from our person'; preposition ἐκ supports 'from.' Meaning is clear; alternative is preference.

last_rejected.why: The subject of 'he says elsewhere' is unclear. In context, it should be Jesus speaking elsewhere in Scripture, but the English 'he says' could grammatically refer to the Father or to the author. The Greek ἀλλαχοῦ φησιν refers to Jesus speaking elsewhere in the Gospel. The English should make clear that Jesus is the speaker: 'he [Jesus] says elsewhere' or 'the Lord says elsewhere.'
last_rejected.ruling: ἀλλαχοῦ φησιν = 'he says elsewhere'; antecedent clear from context. No meaning change; ambiguity is minor.
